opus-5.5.text:
I think the strongest argument comes from looking at what's happened everywhere else in machine learning. Again and again, hand-engineered pipelines with separate modules for perception, state estimation, planning, and control have eventually been overtaken by systems that learn the whole mapping directly from data. We saw it in vision, in speech, and most dramatically in language. Every time you put a human-designed interface between two modules, you're making a bet that you know the right abstraction. In robotics, those abstractions are often wrong, or at least lossy.

Take a classical stack. Perception outputs object poses, the planner reasons over those poses, and the controller executes a trajectory. But a lot of what matters for manipulation doesn't survive that bottleneck. How deformable a cloth is, how a cup's handle is oriented relative to the gripper, whether something is slippery: the pose representation throws that information away, and then every downstream module is working with an impoverished picture of the world. Errors also compound. A small perception error turns into a planning error, which turns into a failed grasp, and there's no gradient flowing back to fix the upstream part.

With an end-to-end model, going from pixels and language to actions, the system learns whatever intermediate representations actually help it get the task done. And you get to ride the scaling curve. If you can collect more diverse data, across more robots, tasks, and environments, the model just keeps improving, without an engineer having to redesign interfaces for every new situation. That's the real unlock for generality. You don't want to hand-build a new pipeline for folding laundry versus loading a dishwasher.

There's also the transfer argument. When you build on top of vision-language models pretrained on internet-scale data, you inherit a lot of semantic understanding of the world for free. The robot can know what a "recyclable item" is or what "the thing you'd use to clean up a spill" means without ever having been explicitly trained on it with robot data. That kind of knowledge flows much more naturally into a single unified model than into a modular stack.

I'd add some caveats, though. End-to-end doesn't mean structureless. There's still a lot of design in the architecture, the action representation, how you handle different control frequencies, and how you combine high-level reasoning with low-level motor control. And the big bottleneck is data. Unlike language, we don't have an internet of robot actions lying around. So the bet on end-to-end is really also a bet that we can solve the data problem through fleets, teleoperation, simulation, and learning from human video. But directionally, I think learning the full mapping is the approach most likely to give us robots that generalize the way we want them to.

r001.rationale: The response describes robotics as challenging and data-limited, but does not characterize it as an AGI-hard problem.

r002.rationale: It argues that modular perception, planning, and control can lose information and compound errors, supporting the view that such a modular architecture is inadequate for general robotic intelligence.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss native audio modeling, vocal expressiveness, or using text as an intermediary for speech.

r004.rationale: It discusses transferring knowledge from vision-language models to robots, but does not frame physical and digital intelligence as expressions of the same underlying intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the core argument comes down to what we've seen work in other domains. If you look at language, if you look at vision, the pattern has been the same every time: people start with carefully engineered pipelines with lots of hand-designed modules, and then eventually a single model trained end-to-end on enough data just outperforms all of that. And I don't think robotics is special in a way that exempts it from that pattern.

The traditional robotics stack is very modular. You have perception, then state estimation, then planning, then control, and each of those is its own research field with its own abstractions. That's great for interpretability and for debugging, but the problem is that every interface between modules is a place where information gets thrown away. Your perception module decides what's relevant before the planner ever sees it. The planner outputs a trajectory in a representation that the controller may or may not be able to execute well. And the errors compound across stages.

With an end-to-end model, you let the model figure out what intermediate representations actually matter for the task, rather than imposing your own guesses about that. And the thing that's really changed recently is that we now have large pretrained models that bring in a huge amount of semantic and commonsense knowledge from the web. So you're not learning physical intelligence from scratch anymore. The robot already has some notion of what a cup is, what "put the cup on the shelf" means, what a kitchen looks like. The end-to-end approach is what lets you actually transfer that knowledge all the way down to actions, instead of bottlenecking it through some hand-designed symbolic interface.

Now, the honest caveat is that data is the hard part. In language you had the whole internet. In robotics you have to collect the data, and it's expensive and slow. So a lot of the research question isn't really "end-to-end versus modular," it's "how do you get enough diverse data for end-to-end to work." But every time we've gotten more data and scaled things up, the end-to-end models have gotten better in ways that were hard to get from engineering more structure in. That's what makes me think it's the right bet.

r002.rationale: It critiques modular robotics pipelines for losing information between stages and argues that end-to-end models can learn task-relevant representations, questioning the modular architecture’s adequacy.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss audio modeling, vocal expressiveness, or a text intermediary.

r004.rationale: It says robotics may follow the same scaling pattern as language and vision, but does not frame physical and digital intelligence as expressions of the same underlying intelligence.

astra-6.text:
I think the appeal is that perception and action are deeply connected. What a robot needs to understand about the world depends on what it’s trying to do. If it’s picking up a cup, it doesn’t just need to recognize that there’s a cup there. It needs to understand where it can grasp it, how the cup might move, and whether that grasp will let it complete the task.

Traditionally, we break that problem into separate components: perception, planning, control. That makes the system easier to reason about, but it also means we have to decide what information passes between those components. And those interfaces can become bottlenecks. You might discard something early that turns out to matter for the action.

An end-to-end model gives you a way to learn those representations together, directly from the task. Potentially, experience from lots of different tasks can improve a shared understanding of how to interact with the world.

I wouldn’t say that makes it automatically the right answer. You still have to deal with safety, data efficiency, and generalization. But it’s a compelling direction because you’re letting the learning process discover which distinctions matter for successful behavior, rather than specifying all of them in advance.

r004.rationale: It discusses physical intelligence without framing it as the same underlying intelligence expressed digitally.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the appeal is that, in the physical world, perception and action are really tightly coupled. What you need to understand about a scene depends on what you’re trying to do. If you’re picking up a cup, you care about its geometry, where you can grasp it, whether there’s something inside it. You don’t necessarily need a complete description of everything in the room.

With a modular system, you make a lot of those decisions ahead of time: this is what perception will represent, this is what the planner will consume, and this is what the controller will execute. Those interfaces can become bottlenecks. An end-to-end model gives you a way to learn the representations that are useful for actually completing the task, with the behavior of the whole system as the objective.

And then there’s the possibility of sharing learning across tasks. Picking up different objects shouldn’t require building entirely separate systems. You want experience with one object or one environment to help you in another.

That doesn’t mean everything has to be one monolithic neural network, or that structure isn’t useful. But I think learning the connection from observations and instructions to actions is a very compelling starting point. The big question is whether we can give it enough diverse experience to generalize reliably beyond the situations it was trained on.

r001.rationale: The response discusses physical robotics tasks and generalization, but does not characterize robotics as an AGI-hard problem.

r002.rationale: It says modular systems set perception, planning, and control interfaces in advance, which can become bottlenecks, and presents end-to-end learning as an alternative for robotic task completion.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss audio modeling, vocal expressiveness, or a text intermediary.

r004.rationale: It does not frame physical and digital intelligence as different expressions of the same underlying intelligence.
